reasons_add: Ibn al-Jawzī's Nuzha reports some exegetes using this very journey as an example in which ahl refers to a wife.
Al-Dāmghānī gives wife and children as a lexical sense of ahl, also mentioning 27:57.

Abū Ḥayyān explains Ibn Muqbil's poetic contrast: khawār breaks apart and dhaʿr is worn wood, unlike the large sturdy fuel. He reports al-Sulamī defining the thick stick as burning or unburning and citing al-Sulamī's verse in which al-jadhā denotes firewood amid an old man's hardship.
Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Farrāʾ deriving jadhwah from cutting off and defining it as wood containing fire without flame.
Abū Ḥayyān cites an unnamed poet using jadhwah for an ember taken from a fire and describing its remaining heat and blaze.

Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī for kasra. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's recognition of all three initial vowels. Ibn al-Jazarī's Nashr assigns kasra to the remaining readers after naming the fatḥa and ḍamma groups.
Ibn Mujāhid and Ibn al-Jazarī both name ʿĀṣim for fatḥa; Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's recognition of all three initial vowels.
Ibn Mujāhid names Ḥamza for ḍamma; Ibn al-Jazarī adds Khalaf. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's recognition of all three initial vowels.

Al-Sāmarrāʾī says Moses' fear in al-Qaṣaṣ makes his promised news tentative, while al-Naml's confident wording fits its less fearful scene; a blazing brand is harder to bring than an ember. He counts ten expressions of hope in al-Qaṣaṣ but only two in al-Naml, making hope a recurring feature of this sūra.

Al-Sāmarrāʾī adds that al-Qaṣaṣ locates the fire at the mountain's side and gives Moses' instruction to wait because its telling develops the scene more fully, whereas al-Naml is concise. He pairs the more specific idkhāl with shihāb qabas and the broader sulūk with jadhwah; a blazing brand is harder to bring than an ember. He also counts ten expressions of hope in al-Qaṣaṣ against two in al-Naml, fitting their tentative and confident promises respectively.

Al-Zarkashī says repeated tellings of Moses and Pharaoh vary in wording, order and detail because each contributes its own nuance; he contrasts Joseph's story collected in one sūra and earlier scripture's separate single tellings.
Al-Sāmarrāʾī locates the closing promise of signs at 27:93 and connects its sayurīkum with Moses' saʾātīkum.

Ibn Mujāhid reports Nāfiʿ opening all but maʿī ridʾan among twelve disputed possessive yāʾs; Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr open nine. Ibn al-Jazarī names Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar for opening laʿallī in six occurrences, and the two Medinans, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr for opening first-person yāʾs in listed Qaṣaṣ phrases, including innī ānastu.

question: 28:29/q28
position: The first-person yāʾ remains quiescent in certain readings of laʿallī and nearby Qaṣaṣ phrases.
reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī reports Yaʿqūb and the Kūfans keeping both occurrences of laʿallī still; he transmits al-Hudhalī's exceptional sukūn in two Qaṣaṣ locations from Ibn Dhakwān through al-Ṣūrī. Ibn Mujāhid reports Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr leaving innī urīd, satajidunī in shāʾ Allāh, and maʿī ridʾan quiescent among twelve disputed possessive yāʾs.
